craft_claim: Because the literal reading is accessed first, a deadpan passage with no key reads as sincere statement or as incompetence before it reads as comedy; the writer must plant at least one unmistakable incongruity so the reader can reframe.

supporting_evidence.note: The most salient meaning — typically the literal one — is accessed first regardless of context, so the deadpan reader arrives at sincerity before irony and needs a salient non-literal target to redirect to. Tier 2; the load-bearing cognitive mechanism for this claim.
Recognition of nonliteral intent is developmentally learned; readers without the competence accept the flat surface at face value. Tier 2; explains why unprepared audiences fail deadpan.

Lexical records show the term's meaning (expressionless delivery, 'pinch without laughing') is conventional but not self-executing — dictionary knowledge does not cue the reader mid-text. Tier 5; recognition only, never sole support.

counterevidence.note: Clark and Gerrig's obviousness spectrum implies cue strength varies by audience: what is unmistakable to a practiced reader may be invisible to a naive one. Bounds the claim: the 'unmistakable tell' must be calibrated to the audience, not absolute.

scope: Written prose addressed to a general readership; strongest in generated or unfamiliar writing where the reader has no author-level prior. Cross-linguistically consistent with Giora's literal-first finding.
exceptions: When the passage is framed by an unmistakably satiric container (a known satirist, a satire venue, an explicit genre label) the key is supplied externally and may be omitted inside the passage.
